paras: The lynching near Millen, Georgia, was the killing in December 1882 of an unnamed Black man whom a mob took from the officers escorting him to jail. He had been arrested and bound over for trial on a charge of attempting to outrage a young white woman. An Augusta wire dispatch carried the case to papers across the country, where shortened copies misnamed the place as "Nelson" or "Wilton."

According to the reports, the woman was walking through the woods from her father's house to her brother-in-law's, half a mile away, when a man accosted her. He was said to have tried to choke her and to have cut her twice across the breast, severing her clothes, before her calls for help frightened him off. The Waynesboro correspondent of the Savannah Morning News added that she was not seriously injured.

The accused man was caught and bound over for trial. On the way to jail, the posse in charge of him was overpowered, and in the wire's words "the mob took him from the officers and lynched him." None of the reports names the man, the woman, the officers or any member of the mob, and only one later roundup states that he was hanged.
No report of an inquest, arrests or other official response appears in the coverage.

The earliest account came in a Waynesboro letter dated December 19 and printed in the Savannah Morning News on December 21, under the heading "A Negro Fiend Lynched." Its writer called the man a "wretch" and said he had been "disposed of by Judge Lynch," placing the lynching on the day of writing.

An Augusta dispatch dated December 22 then ran in papers from Washington and New York to Knoxville and Lancaster, under headlines such as "Lynch Law in Georgia" and "A Negro Miscreant Lynched." Shorter versions reached Dakota, California and Maine, often as one line in a news summary, and these give the town as "Nelson" or "Wilton." Weekly roundups kept the story in print later in the month, the Watertown Republican under "Nelson, Ga." and The Bee under Millen in its "Southern News" column.
None of these papers questioned the accusation or criticized the mob, and the Black press of the period is not represented in the coverage.

Accounts differ on the date: the Waynesboro letter places the lynching on December 19, while later wire items say "Thursday" (December 21) or "the 22d." The Stanford, Kentucky, Interior Journal alone said he was "taken from jail by a mob," against the fuller reports that he was seized on the way to jail. The letter written near the scene is the earliest and closest source, and the fuller wire text agrees with it on Millen as the place.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News correspondent headed it 'A Negro Fiend Lynched' and called the man a 'wretch' disposed of 'by Judge Lynch'.
Northern and western papers ran the Augusta wire under heads such as 'Lynch Law in Georgia', 'A Negro Miscreant Lynched', and 'Negro Lynched', calling him a 'miscreant'.

conflicts.note: The local Waynesboro letter and the fuller wire text both say Millen; 'Nelson' and 'Wilton' appear only in shortened copies of the same Augusta dispatch and look like telegraphic corruptions.
The Dec. 19 letter written nearby is the earliest source; the later dates track the Dec. 22 dateline of the wire dispatch.
